name: To Whoever Finds This First
author: Name withheld
description: A handwritten letter, photocopied and left folded inside a battered hardcase at a dead drop location in the Shelf-7 Narrows transition corridor, dated approximately six weeks after the disappearance of a freelancer known by the handle Cassowary. The original was presumably kept by the author. Circulated among brokers in the mid-corridor network as an informal artifact — not for distribution, but passed hand to hand anyway, the way these things are. No author name is given. The letter is addressed to whoever opens the case first.
body:
To whoever finds this first —

I don't know you. You might not have known him well either. That's fine. I'm not asking you to grieve. I'm asking you to do a few practical things and then I'm asking you to pass something along, and I understand that's already more than most people want from a stranger's letter shoved in a hardcase.

Here's how I know something was wrong. Not when he missed the check-in window — he'd missed those before, a few hours here and there, and I'd learned what that felt like and what to do with it, which is mostly nothing, mostly just keeping your hands busy. Not the first day. Not the second. It was the third morning, when I woke up and noticed I'd stopped listening for the door. I don't know how to explain that better. At some point my body decided before I did. I'd been sleeping light for two years — you learn to, with this — and then suddenly I wasn't anymore. I slept like something had been resolved. That's when I knew.

I want to say something about what it was like, the two years before that, because I don't think people who haven't lived it understand and I want someone to understand before I finish writing this.

He didn't tell me things. That was the arrangement, not because he didn't trust me, but because knowing created exposure and because there is no such thing as accidentally saying the wrong thing to the wrong person if you genuinely don't know anything. I understood this. I agreed to it. I made my peace with it in stages, every few months, every time the peace wore thin. What you don't understand until you're in it is that not knowing is not the same as not wondering. I built a whole architecture of inference — if he came back quiet, it went badly. If he came back hungry, it went well. If he cleaned his kit the same night, something scared him. If he left the case by the door instead of stowing it, he was going out again soon. Two years of reading those signals, none of which he meant to send, probably, but there they were.

I'm telling you this because I want you to understand that I am not a person who was kept in the dark. I chose the dark. I kept myself there carefully because it was the safer thing for both of us. I am not angry about that. I want to be clear about that: I am not angry about that particular thing.

Here is what needs to happen with his equipment.

The Korvath-Saito carbine — matte black, left side of the case, wrapped in the green cloth — goes to a woman who goes by Perdrix. She operates out of a drop in Shelf-4, near the water reclaim junction, and she'll know what it is when she sees it. He owed her and this clears it. Don't negotiate, don't hold it, just give it to her.

The neural overlay kit — the older model, the one with the cracked housing on the left lead — I want sold. Whatever you get is yours for doing this. It's worth more than you'll get for it but I don't have the contacts he had and I don't want it in this apartment anymore. The port diagnostic tool that goes with it, the small one with the yellow tape around the handle, keep that out. That one goes with the message I'll describe in a moment.

The rest — the clothes, the secondary kit, the personal items — I have already dealt with. I'm not asking you to do anything with those. I did that part myself, before I wrote this, and I don't want to talk about it.

His boots are not in the case. I kept the boots. I'm allowed to keep something.

Now: the broker.

His name is Renk and he runs a walk-in out of a freight office in the Canopy-2 service corridor, the one attached to the old Matsudara cold storage. I don't want you to hurt him. I want to be specific about this because I understand the impulse and I'm not asking for it. What I want is for someone to go and look him in the face and say that Cassowary's name should be said clearly, not quietly, and that whoever vouched for the contract is being asked to vouch for what happened on it. That's all. That's the language. I know what it means in the network and he'll know I know and that is enough for me. That is the thing I am asking for. You can tell him who sent you or not. It doesn't matter.

If he denies the contract existed, walk away. He's protected higher than I can reach and I know that. I am not asking for justice. I am asking for the record to exist somewhere, in someone's head, because that is the only kind of record that doesn't get erased.

Last thing.

There is a person — I don't know her real name, I only know she's called Sable, and that she works A-tier out of the mid-corridor network, and that she and Cassowary had a history I was not given details of and did not ask for. I don't know if you can find her. I don't know if she even knows yet.

If you can reach her: tell her there is no bad feeling. Tell her specifically that — no bad feeling from me. He talked about her occasionally, the way you talk about someone you once trusted entirely and still do despite everything, and I made my peace with that too, in stages, the way I made my peace with everything about this life that wasn't mine to control. She deserves to know he's gone, and she deserves to know it from someone who isn't angry.

Give her the diagnostic tool with the yellow tape. He'd want her to have something functional. He was practical like that.

That's everything I need from you.

I don't know who you are. You might be someone who knew him well and is reading this through your own grief and if so I'm sorry to hand you tasks, I know that's not what you need right now. Or you might be a stranger who found a hardcase and is reading this confused and mildly annoyed. Either way, thank you for reading to the end. Thank you for knowing his name was Cassowary, even if that's the only thing you know about him.

He was not a good man in the way that word gets used by people who haven't had to make the choices he made. He was a good man in the way that actually matters, which is specific and hard to explain and which I do not owe anyone an explanation of.

I am going to be fine. I want to write that down so it exists somewhere even if I don't fully believe it yet. I am going to be fine.

Leave the hardcase somewhere useful. Don't let it go to waste.

— Name withheld
